gospel.d: ‘Good news’ (Greek euangelion). In the New Testament it means the announcement of what God has done in Jesus Christ: his death for our sins, his resurrection, and his reign as Lord (1 Corinthians 15:1–5), with the call to repent and believe. All Christian traditions agree on this core. They differ on how a person receives what the gospel offers (see justification, faith).

grace.d: God’s undeserved favour and kindness, given freely and not earned. In Paul it is the opposite of wages (Romans 4:4; 11:6): salvation is a gift from start to finish (Ephesians 2:8–9).

v.t: Grace is God’s sovereign kindness. For those he saves, God’s grace does not merely make salvation possible but actually brings them to faith. The Spirit effectively draws them to Christ, ‘yet so as they come most freely’ (Westminster Confession 10.1).
Grace goes before every person (‘prevenient grace’), freeing the will enough to respond to God. Without it no one can turn to God, but it can be resisted (Remonstrance, 1610, art. 4).

Grace is both God’s favour and a real gift of new life poured into the soul (‘sanctifying grace’), first given in baptism and nourished through the sacraments. It can be lost through grave sin and restored through penance.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 10

justification.d: God’s act of declaring a person ‘righteous’, that is, in the right with him and accepted. It is a law-court word: the opposite of condemnation (Romans 8:33–34). Paul’s central claim is that we are justified by grace, through faith in Christ, not by doing what the law requires (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28).

v.t: A once-for-all legal verdict. God pardons all our sins and accepts us as righteous, not for anything done in us, but by counting (‘imputing’) Christ’s obedience and death to us, received by faith alone. The inner change of sanctification always follows but is distinct (Westminster Confession 11.1).
The same Reformation teaching: we are freely justified for Christ’s sake through faith, not by our own merits or works (Augsburg Confession, art. 4).

Justification is by grace through faith alone. Wesley wrote: ‘The plain scriptural notion of justification is pardon, the forgiveness of sins.’ Faith is the condition God has appointed for receiving it.

Justification is ‘not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man’. It is first given in baptism, can grow, and can be lost and restored. Nothing before justification, whether faith or works, earns it (Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 7–8).

works-of-the-law.d: Paul’s phrase (Galatians 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10; Romans 3:20, 28) for doing what the law of Moses requires. Paul insists no one is justified this way. The phrase also appears in a Dead Sea Scroll (4QMMT), so it was real Jewish vocabulary of the time.

v.t: Obedience to the whole law, moral as well as ceremonial, as a basis for being accepted by God (Luther, Calvin; today, for example, Schreiner).
The whole law, but especially as it marked Jews off from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws, Sabbath (Dunn, Wright).
The ceremonial law only (Origen and Jerome, as Calvin reports). Calvin rejected this as too narrow.

faith.d: Trust in God and his promises, above all trust in Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. In the New Testament faith is not a meritorious work that earns salvation, but the empty hand that receives it (Romans 4:4–5). True faith is never idle: it ‘expresses itself through love’ (Galatians 5:6).

v.t: Saving faith is itself a gift of God, worked by the Spirit in those he calls (Westminster Confession 14.1).
Faith is made possible by God’s grace, which goes before it, but it is a real human response that a person could refuse. God has appointed faith as the condition of salvation.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 11 (justification) and ch. 17 (perseverance), OPC text
The Five Arminian Articles (Remonstrance, 1610), in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 3

righteousness.d: Being right with God, measured by his standard. In Paul it can mean God’s own faithfulness to do what is right and to save (Romans 3:21–26), or the right standing God gives to those who believe (Philippians 3:9). Abraham ‘believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’ (Genesis 15:6; Galatians 3:6).

election.d: God’s choosing of people for salvation and for his purposes. Scripture plainly teaches that God chooses (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 8:29–30). Christians differ over the basis of that choice.

v.t: Before creation God freely chose particular people to be saved in Christ, ‘without any foresight of faith, or good works’ in them (Westminster Confession 3.5). His grace then brings them to faith.

God chose to save all who would believe in Christ (Remonstrance, art. 1). His choosing of individuals rests on his foreknowledge of their faith; or election is mainly the choice of a people, the church in Christ, which individuals join by faith.
Both affirm God’s predestining grace while insisting on genuine human freedom to cooperate or resist. Catholic theology contains a range of views on how the two fit together.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 3
The Five Arminian Articles (Remonstrance, 1610), in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 3

atonement.d: How Christ’s death reconciles sinners to God (‘at-one-ment’). The New Testament uses several pictures for it: sacrifice, ransom, redemption, bearing the curse, victory over evil powers. Christians hold these together.

v.t: At its centre is penal substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty our sins deserved (Galatians 3:13; Isaiah 53:5).

Most also affirm that Christ died in our place, for every person, though only believers receive the benefit (Remonstrance, art. 2). Some prefer to describe it as satisfying God’s moral government of the world.
Orthodox theology characteristically puts the emphasis on Christ’s victory over sin, death and the devil, and the healing of human nature, rather than on legal categories.

src.l: The Five Arminian Articles (Remonstrance, 1610), in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 3

redemption.d: Being set free by the payment of a price, like a slave bought out of slavery. Christ ‘redeemed us from the curse of the law’ (Galatians 3:13), and ‘those under the law’ (4:5), at the cost of his own life.

covenant.d: A binding relationship established by God with promises and obligations: with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, David, and the ‘new covenant’ in Christ (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20). In Galatians Paul sets the promise-covenant with Abraham, fulfilled in Christ, against the Sinai covenant as a way of standing before God.

v.t: Reads the whole Bible through the covenants. Many Reformed theologians speak of one ‘covenant of grace’ running through the Old and New Testaments in different forms.
Stresses clearer distinctions between God’s dealings with Israel and with the church.

law.d: Usually the law of Moses, the commands given at Sinai (Exodus–Deuteronomy). Sometimes it means the books of Moses as Scripture (Galatians 4:21). Paul calls it ‘holy, righteous and good’ (Romans 7:12) but insists it cannot give life or justify a sinner.

v.t: Traditionally distinguishes moral, ceremonial and civil law. The ceremonies are fulfilled in Christ; the moral law, summarised in the Ten Commandments, still guides Christian life (Westminster Confession ch. 19).
Stresses the contrast between law (what God demands, which exposes sin) and gospel (what God gives in Christ).

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 19

adoption.d: God’s act of making believers his children and heirs (Galatians 4:5; Romans 8:15). In Roman law an adopted son had full rights of inheritance. Believers share in the Son’s own relationship with the Father, and the Spirit leads them to call God ‘Abba, Father’.

perseverance.d: Whether a true believer will certainly continue in faith to the end, or can fall away and be lost. Scripture contains both strong promises of God keeping his people (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6) and serious warnings (Galatians 5:4; Hebrews 6:4–6).

v.t: Those truly united to Christ ‘can neither totally nor finally fall away’ but will be kept to the end (Westminster Confession 17.1). The warnings are real means God uses to keep them.
A true believer can turn from Christ and be finally lost (Wesley). The Remonstrance of 1610 left the question open; later Arminians generally affirmed the possibility.
Grace can be lost through grave (‘mortal’) sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance (Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 14).

flesh.d: In Paul’s moral sense, not the physical body but human nature turned in on itself and away from God (Galatians 5:16–21; Romans 8:5–8). Sometimes it simply means ordinary human life or descent (Galatians 2:20; 4:23).

sanctification.d: Being made holy. In one sense believers are already set apart for God (1 Corinthians 6:11). In another they are being changed, by the Spirit, into the likeness of Christ throughout life (2 Corinthians 3:18).

v.t: Sanctification always follows justification but is distinct from it, and remains imperfect in this life (Westminster Confession ch. 13).
Holds out the hope of ‘entire sanctification’ or ‘Christian perfection’ in this life: a heart wholly filled with love for God and neighbour. It is not freedom from all mistakes.
Sanctification is part of justification itself, the inner renewal of the person by grace.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 13
Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification (1547), chs. 7–8, 14, in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 2

son-of-man.d: In Hebrew and Aramaic, ‘son of man’ ordinarily means ‘a human being’ (as often in Ezekiel and Psalm 8:4). In Daniel 7:13 ‘one like a son of man’ comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus used ‘the Son of Man’ as his main title for himself, both of his humble mission and suffering (Mark 10:45) and of his coming glory (Mark 14:62). It holds together his real humanity and his divine authority, and it did not carry the political overtones of ‘Messiah’.

src.l: ‘Son of Man’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

apocalyptic.d: From the Greek for ‘revelation’ or ‘unveiling’. It is a type of writing in which hidden heavenly realities and the future are revealed, often through visions, symbolic beasts and numbers, and angelic interpreters. Examples include Daniel 7–12, Revelation, and many Jewish writings of the period between the Testaments. Its symbols are meant to be decoded, not read literally, and its main message is that God is in control and will bring history to its goal.

antichrist.d: The word appears only in 1 and 2 John, of a coming opponent of Christ and of the many ‘antichrists’ already present (1 John 2:18). Christians have long linked it with Daniel’s little horn and final king, Paul’s ‘man of lawlessness’ (2 Thessalonians 2), and the beast of Revelation 13.

v.t: A single, final, personal enemy of God who will appear before Christ’s return (common among premillennial and dispensational Christians, and held by many others).

The principle of opposition to Christ embodied in many figures and powers through history, possibly culminating in a final one (many amillennial interpreters). The Reformers often identified Antichrist with the papacy; that view is now rare outside some confessional traditions.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

messiah.d: Hebrew mashiach, Greek christos: ‘anointed one’. In the Old Testament kings and priests were anointed with oil for their office. The prophets came to promise one coming king from David’s line who would rule for ever. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as this Messiah, the Christ.

resurrection.d: Being raised bodily from death to life. Daniel 12:2 is the clearest Old Testament statement of a future resurrection of the dead to one of two destinies. Jesus’ own bodily resurrection is the centre of the Christian faith and the pattern and guarantee of the resurrection of his people (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). It is affirmed by all historic Christian creeds (‘the resurrection of the body’).

wrath.d: God’s settled, holy opposition to sin and evil. It is not a loss of temper, but the response of a good God to what destroys his creation and his creatures. Paul speaks of it as both present (Romans 1:18) and future (2:5), and of Christ rescuing believers from it (5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

sin.d: Falling short of God’s glory and breaking his law (Romans 3:23; 1 John 3:4). It is both acts we commit and a power or condition that enslaves (Romans 6; 7:14). At root it is refusing to honour God as God and putting created things in his place (Romans 1:21–25).

propitiation.d: The Greek hilastērion (Romans 3:25) and related words (1 John 2:2; 4:10). In the Greek Old Testament it is the ‘mercy seat’ on the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. ‘Propitiation’ means turning away wrath; ‘expiation’ means wiping away sin.

v.t: Christ’s death is a propitiation: it satisfies God’s justice and turns away his wrath from those who believe, because Christ bore the penalty in their place.
Prefer expiation, or the ‘mercy seat’ picture, stressing that God himself provides the means of dealing with sin. Many hold that both ideas are present.

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

imputation.d: Crediting something to someone’s account (Greek logizomai, ‘to count’, ‘to credit’; Romans 4). Abraham’s faith was ‘credited to him as righteousness’.

v.t: Three imputations: Adam’s sin to his descendants, believers’ sin to Christ, and Christ’s righteousness to believers (Westminster Confession 6.3; 11.1).
Strongly affirms that Christ’s righteousness is credited to the believer through faith.
Affirms that believers are justified freely for Christ’s sake, with faith counted for righteousness; often more cautious about saying Christ’s active obedience itself is transferred.
Holds that justification includes a righteousness actually given to, and at work in, the believer, not only credited.

original-sin.d: The effect of the first sin of Adam on the whole human race: all are born into a condition of sinfulness and death (Romans 5:12–21; Psalm 51:5). All historic Christian traditions affirm that humanity is fallen; they differ on whether Adam’s guilt itself is passed on.

v.t: Adam’s guilt is imputed to all his descendants, and a corrupted nature is passed on (Westminster Confession 6.3).
Original sin is ‘contracted’, not ‘committed’: the loss of original holiness and a wounded nature inclined to sin, taken away in baptism (Catechism 404–405).
Speaks of ‘ancestral sin’: all inherit death and corruption from Adam, but not his personal guilt.
Affirms a corrupted nature that cannot turn to God without grace; views differ on inherited guilt.

reconciliation.d: The restoring of a broken relationship (Greek katallassō). Through Christ’s death God reconciles to himself people who were his enemies (Romans 5:10–11; 2 Corinthians 5:18–21). It is God who takes the initiative.

incarnation.d: God the Son becoming fully human (‘the Word became flesh’, John 1:14), without ceasing to be God. Christians confess one person, Jesus Christ, with two complete natures, divine and human, neither mixed nor divided (Definition of Chalcedon, AD 451). This is shared ground for Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians alike.

trinity.d: The one God exists eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet there is only one God. The word is not in the Bible, but the church found the truth there: one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), the Father is God, the Son is God (John 1:1; 20:28), the Spirit is God (Acts 5:3–4), and the three are distinct (Matthew 28:19). Confessed in the Nicene Creed (AD 325/381) by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches. Jehovah’s Witnesses and some other groups reject it.

src.l: Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381), in Schaff vol. 2

regeneration.d: The work of the Holy Spirit giving new spiritual life to a person, so that they are ‘born again’ or ‘born from above’ (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5). All agree it is God’s work, not human achievement. They differ on how it relates to faith and baptism.

v.t: The Spirit gives new life first, and as a result the person believes. Regeneration is God’s sovereign act, which people cannot cause or resist (Westminster Confession 10.1–2).
God’s ‘prevenient’ grace, going before, enables every person to respond; the new birth follows faith. Wesley saw baptism as its ‘outward sign and means’, ‘wherever baptism can be had’.
God ordinarily gives the new birth through baptism. The Catholic Catechism says baptism ‘signifies and actually brings about the birth of water and the Spirit’ (1215).

holy-spirit.d: The third person of the Trinity, fully God with the Father and the Son. Jesus calls him ‘another Advocate’ (Greek paraklētos: helper, counsellor, one called alongside), ‘the Spirit of truth’, who lives in believers, teaches, reminds, convicts the world and glorifies Christ (John 14–16). He is a person, not an impersonal force.

v.t: Confess that the Spirit proceeds ‘from the Father and the Son’ (Latin filioque), a phrase added to the Nicene Creed in the West. The Catholic Catechism acknowledges that it was not in the Creed of 381 and calls the Eastern and Western formulas a ‘legitimate complementarity’ (246–248).

Confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, as John 15:26 says, and reject the Western addition to the Creed. Orthodox teaching cites John of Damascus: the Spirit is ‘from the Father’, and is called ‘the Spirit of the Son’ but not said to be ‘from the Son’.

lords-supper.d: The meal of bread and wine that Jesus gave his followers on the night he was betrayed, saying ‘This is My body’ and ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood’, and ‘do this in remembrance of Me’ (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Paul calls it a ‘participation’ in Christ’s body and blood (10:16). All Christians keep it; they differ on how Christ is present.

v.t: By the consecration ‘there takes place a change of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ’ (Catechism 1376), called transubstantiation; Christ is ‘truly, really, and substantially contained’ (1374).

The bread and wine are ‘changed, or transubstantiated, into the very Body of Christ, and into the very Blood of Christ’, but the word does not define how; the manner is a mystery ‘none can understand but God’ (Longer Catechism 339–340).
‘It is the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the bread and wine’ (Luther’s Small Catechism), without the bread ceasing to be bread.

Believers ‘spiritually, receive, and feed upon, Christ crucified’ (Westminster Confession 29.7). For Calvin the sign is not empty: ‘the reality is here conjoined with the sign’, by the Spirit, though Christ’s body is not locally present.

Many Baptist and other evangelical churches stress the Supper as a remembrance and proclamation of Christ’s death (‘do this in remembrance of Me’; ‘you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes’), with Christ present among his people by his Spirit rather than in the bread and wine.

spiritual-gifts.w: Spiritual gifts (and whether some have ceased)
spiritual-gifts.d: Abilities and activities the Holy Spirit gives to believers ‘for the common good’ (1 Corinthians 12:7): Paul’s lists include wisdom, teaching, helping, leading and giving, as well as prophecy, healing, miracles, tongues and interpretation (1 Corinthians 12; Romans 12; Ephesians 4). Christians agree the Spirit still gives gifts. They differ on whether the more miraculous gifts continue today.

v.t: Held by many Reformed and some other evangelicals. The miraculous gifts were ‘part of the credentials of the Apostles’ and ‘necessarily passed away with’ the apostolic church (B. B. Warfield). The Westminster Confession speaks of God’s ‘former ways’ of revealing his will as ‘now ceased’ (1.1).

All the gifts continue until Christ returns, since Paul says partial things pass away ‘when the perfect comes’ (13:10), which most take to mean Christ’s return. Held by many evangelicals across denominations, often with a call to test prophecy carefully.
Baptism in the Spirit is ‘an experience distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth’, and ‘the initial physical evidence’ of it is speaking in tongues (Assemblies of God).

millennium.d: The ‘thousand years’ of Revelation 20:1–6, during which Satan is bound and faithful believers ‘reigned with Christ’. It is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible, and Christians read it in several ways. All agree that Christ will return in person, raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new.

v.t: Christ returns before (‘pre’) a future thousand-year reign on earth. Held by early writers such as Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus (‘historic premillennialism’). Dispensational premillennialism adds a rapture of the church before a seven-year tribulation, and a restoration of national Israel (for example Dallas Theological Seminary: ‘He will thus introduce the millennial age; bind Satan and place him in the abyss’).

The thousand years is a symbol for the present age between Christ’s first and second comings: Satan is bound so that the gospel goes to the nations, and believers who have died reign with Christ. Augustine, who once held a millennial view, came to teach that ‘the Church even now is the kingdom of Christ’. Aquinas, Luther and Calvin took this view, and it is widely held in Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed churches.
Christ returns after (‘post’) a long golden age in which the gospel spreads and transforms the world. The Puritans were notable supporters.

The Church ‘has rejected even modified forms of this falsification of the kingdom to come under the name of millenarianism’ (Catechism 676), that is, any expectation of a perfect kingdom achieved within history before the last judgement.
Wesley held that ‘two distinct thousand years are mentioned throughout this whole passage’.

kingdom-of-god.d: God’s reign: his rule as king, rather than a territory. The Old Testament looked for the day when God would act to put the world right and rule openly through his anointed king. Jesus announced that this time had come with him: ‘The time is fulfilled…and the kingdom of God is near’ (Mark 1:15). His healings and exorcisms were signs of it. Yet it grows quietly like a seed (Mark 4:26–32) and will come in full only when the Son of Man returns. Theologians often summarise this as ‘already, and not yet’. Matthew usually says ‘kingdom of heaven’, a reverent Jewish way of saying the same thing.

src.l: ‘Gospels’ (incl. the Synoptic problem), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

baptism.d: Washing with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), the rite by which people are received into the church. Jesus himself was baptised by John (Mark 1:9), and the apostles baptised those who believed (Acts 2:38–41). All the main traditions practise it; they differ on who should be baptised and what it does.

v.t: Baptism truly forgives original and personal sins and gives new birth. ‘The Lord himself affirms that Baptism is necessary for salvation’ for those who have heard the gospel and could ask for it (Catechism 1257). Infants are baptised, since they too need ‘the new birth in Baptism’ (1250).

Baptism is a sacrament in which a believer, ‘having his body thrice plunged in water’, ‘is born again of the Holy Ghost to a life spiritual and holy’. Infants are baptised ‘for the faith of their parents and sponsors’ (Longer Catechism 288–292).

Baptism ‘worketh forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives everlasting salvation to all who believe’; not the water itself, ‘but the Word of God’ with the water, received by faith (Luther’s Small Catechism, citing Mark 16:16). Infants are baptised.

A sign and seal of the covenant of grace. ‘The infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized’, as infants received circumcision. But ‘grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed unto it’ that no one can be saved without it (Westminster Confession 28.4–5).

Baptism is for those ‘who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ’, by immersion (1689 Baptist Confession 29.2, 4). It is an act of obedience and testimony that follows faith, and is not given to infants. Many Pentecostal and independent churches agree.

intermediate-state.d: What happens to a person between death and the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return. Most Christians have held that the soul lives on consciously, either with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8) or apart from him (Luke 16:23), awaiting the resurrection, when body and soul are reunited for the final judgment. The final hope is not the soul in heaven but the resurrection of the body.

v.t: Souls ‘neither die nor sleep’ but ‘immediately return to God’: the righteous, ‘made perfect in holiness’, are received into heaven; the wicked are cast into hell. ‘Besides these two places…the Scripture acknowledgeth none’ (Westminster Confession 32.1).
Wesley called Abraham’s bosom ‘paradise; the place where the souls of good men remain from death to the resurrection’ (note on Luke 16:22).

Each person is judged at death in a ‘particular judgment’: ‘either entrance into the blessedness of heaven—through a purification or immediately,—or immediate and everlasting damnation’ (Catechism 1022). That purification is called purgatory (1030–1031).

‘The souls of the righteous are in light and rest, with a foretaste of eternal happiness; but the souls of the wicked are in a state the reverse of this.’ Full happiness waits for the resurrection, and the departed may be helped by the church’s prayers (Longer Catechism 372–376, citing Luke 16:22).

Seventh-day Adventists, and some others, hold that the dead are not conscious: ‘Until that day death is an unconscious state for all people’ (Fundamental Belief 26). They usually read Luke 16 as a parable not meant to describe the afterlife.

saints.d: In the Bible, ‘saints’ (Greek hagioi, ‘holy ones’) means all of God’s people, not an especially holy few. Paul calls whole churches ‘saints’, even troubled ones like Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:2, where the BSB has ‘holy’). Believers are holy first because God has set them apart for himself in Christ; growing in holy living follows from that.

v.t: All believers are saints, united to Christ and to one another (Westminster Confession 26.1). Faithful Christians of the past are honoured as examples, but prayer and worship are given to God alone, ‘not to angels, saints, or any other creature’ (21.2).

All the faithful are called saints, and the Church also ‘canonizes’ some: it solemnly recognises that they lived lives of heroic virtue and proposes them ‘as models and intercessors’ (Catechism 828; compare 956).

overseer.d: An ‘overseer’ (Greek episkopos, the word from which ‘bishop’ comes) leads a local church, teaching it and caring for it like a shepherd. In the New Testament ‘overseer’ and ‘elder’ describe the same people (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7); the New Bible Dictionary judges the two terms ‘synonymous in the NT’. Their qualifications are set out in 1 Timothy 3:1–7 and Titus 1:5–9.

v.t: Each local church is led by a group of elders (overseers), one of whom is often the main pastor; Presbyterians also have wider councils of elders. Many Baptist churches have a pastor, or a team of elders, with deacons.
Keep bishops as a separate order above elders (priests). Catholic teaching holds that bishops are successors of the apostles (Catechism 861–862).

deacon.d: From the Greek diakonos, ‘servant’, often a table-servant. Most New Testament uses of the word simply mean someone who serves; Paul even calls himself a diakonos of the gospel. In a few places, such as Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8–13, it names a recognised role in the church alongside the overseers. Churches differ on what deacons do today, but practical and caring service is at its heart.

src.l: ‘Deacon’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

circumcision.d: Cutting away the foreskin. God gave it to Abraham as the sign of his covenant (Genesis 17). In Paul’s day some Jewish believers taught that non-Jewish Christians had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people. Paul rejected this (Galatians 5:2–6; Philippians 3:2–3). What matters is a heart changed by God’s Spirit, which the Old Testament itself called for (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Romans 2:28–29).

src.l: ‘Circumcision’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

gentiles.d: Anyone who is not Jewish. The Hebrew and Greek words simply mean ‘nations’. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3). By Jesus’ time some Jews used ‘Gentile’ as a term of scorn. Much of the New Testament is about Gentiles being welcomed into God’s people through faith in Christ, without first becoming Jews (Acts 15; Ephesians 2:11–22).

src.l: ‘Gentiles’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

pharisees.d: A Jewish party, active from around 150 BC, known for keeping the law of Moses strictly, together with a large body of spoken tradition about how to keep it. The name probably comes from a word meaning ‘to separate’. Paul was a Pharisee before he met Christ (Philippians 3:5; Acts 23:6). Jesus often clashed with Pharisees, though some, like Nicodemus, were open to him (John 3:1–2).

src.l: ‘Pharisees’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

apostle.d: From the Greek apostolos, ‘one who is sent’, a messenger commissioned to act for the one who sends him. Above all it means the Twelve whom Jesus chose, and Paul, whom the risen Christ called; they were the founding witnesses and teachers of the church (Ephesians 2:20). The word is also used more loosely of messengers sent by churches; in Philippians 2:25 Epaphroditus is the Philippians’ apostolos, their ‘messenger’.

src.l: ‘Apostle’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

sacrifice.d: Something offered to God. In the Old Testament, animals, grain and drink offerings were brought to God for worship, thanks and the covering of sin (Leviticus 1–7). The New Testament teaches that Christ’s death was the one perfect sacrifice for sin, offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Christians now offer ‘sacrifices’ of a different kind: themselves (Romans 12:1), praise, and doing good and sharing (Hebrews 13:15–16).

src.l: ‘Sacrifice and Offering’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

repentance.d: Turning around: a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin and back to God. The Old Testament’s main word means ‘return’; the New Testament word means a change of mind. It is more than feeling sorry; it shows itself in a changed life (Matthew 3:8). John the Baptist and Jesus both began their preaching with ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near’ (3:2; 4:17). Repentance and faith belong together (Mark 1:15).

v.t: ‘Repentance unto life is an evangelical grace’, God’s gift. It is not ‘any satisfaction for sin, or any cause of the pardon thereof’, which is God’s free grace in Christ, ‘yet it is of such necessity to all sinners, that none may expect pardon without it’ (Westminster Confession 15.1, 3).

‘Interior repentance is a radical reorientation of our whole life’, a conversion to God with all our heart (Catechism 1431). It is expressed in many ways, and especially in the sacrament of Penance (confession).

sadducees.d: One of the main Jewish parties in Jesus’ day, closely linked with the temple and the high priests. They accepted the authority of the Scriptures but not the oral traditions of the Pharisees, and they denied the resurrection of the dead (Matthew 22:23; Acts 23:8). They disappear from history after the temple was destroyed in AD 70. Little of their own writing survives, so we know them mainly through their opponents.

src.l: ‘Sadducees’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

scribes.d: Experts in the Law of Moses. In Jesus’ day scribes copied, studied and taught the Scriptures and the traditions built around them, and acted as lawyers and judges in local disputes. Many were Pharisees. They taught by quoting earlier teachers in a chain of tradition going back, they said, to Moses (Mishnah, Avot 1:1). The crowds were amazed that Jesus taught ‘as one who had authority, and not as their scribes’ (Matthew 7:29). Some scribes became his disciples (Matthew 13:52); many opposed him (Matthew 23).

hypocrite.d: From the Greek word for an actor on the stage, someone who wore a mask and played a part. In the Gospels a hypocrite is someone whose religion is a performance: outward show without inward reality, done to win people’s praise (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16), or someone who judges others while ignoring his own faults (Matthew 7:5). Jesus uses the word more often in Matthew than in any other Gospel, especially of the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23).
